item.description: Stanford Events — Boil, boil, toil and trouble… what bewitching book will you find at the Education Library? Our witchy book display has a little bit of magic for everyone! item.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
item.description: Stanford Events — The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future. The exhibition explores Kim’s concept of “Indigenous Futures” through art as a form of civilizational transformation, expressing p'owŏl (포월 抱越), embracing and transcending the pain and contradictions of reality while reaching toward new possibilities for the future. The opening reception on October 8 will feature an artist talk and a Korean mask dance (탈춤 t'alch'um) performance by Kim Bong-Jun and Che Se-hyun, a Seattle-based creative director and multidisciplinary artist. item.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
item.description: Stanford Events — Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France. Though commercially unsuccessful, these experiments laid the groundwork for the scanning, machining, and printing technologies ubiquitous today. Bringing together these rare artifacts, the exhibition opens up a little-known chapter of history to reveal the roots and richness of our contemporary world. An accompanying catalogue features four newly commissioned essays accompanied by previously unpublished documentation,

item.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
item.description: Stanford Events — Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day. The exhibition includes microscope images revealing the textile structure of the woven text as well as a woven enlargement that illustrates its basic principles, along with several artworks inspired by or related to the themes of the exhibition. Location: Green Library, Bing Wing

item.title: Electric Contrasts: the Art of the Detail
item.description: Stanford Events — Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail brings together photobooks and magazines to show how the revolution of photography in the late 19th and early 20th century changed the history of art. Electric Contrasts takes Kenneth Clark’s landmark 1938 book One Hundred Details from Pictures in the National Gallery as a starting point to illuminate the impact black and white photographic details of Old Master paintings had on new ways of seeing in the early 20th century. The exhibition reveals the anachronistic and provocative juxtapositions of artworks in avant-garde magazines and books which created a radically new vision that would go on to influence television and the internet. Curated by Altair Brandon-Salmon. Bowes Art & Architecture Library hours: M-Th 9-7pm; Friday 9-5pm; Sunday 12-6pm. Tour by Dr. Brandon-Salmon on 9/5 at 6 pm prior to Electric Contrasts Study Evening. Location: McMurtry Building

item.title: The Frontier Between Legendary Monsters and Verified Natural History
item.description: Stanford Events — Have you ever looked at a mysterious lake shadow and thought, "Is that a giant prehistoric plesiosaur, or just an extraordinarily dramatic floating log?" If so, step into the corridors of the Science Library for our featured book display exploring where ancient myth meets rigorous evolutionary biology. We’re separating biological facts from blurry photographs, blurry folklore, and very clear hoaxes. Come for the ancient folklore, stay for the cold, hard science—and remember: the truth is in here, but so are the quiet study hours. Location: Sapp Center for Science Teaching and Learning

item.title: A Vision of Paris: The Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford
item.description: Stanford Events — Stanford University Libraries presents A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford, on view in the Peterson Gallery and Munger Rotunda of the Cecil H. Green Library from September 22, 2026 to January 24, 2027. Roxane Debuisson (1927–2018) dedicated sixty years to documenting the transformation of the city of Paris during the nineteenth century. If Roxane Debuisson could not stop the changes she saw underway in the late 20th century, she could at least preserve the city’s earlier history through images, literature, guidebooks, and other documents. Her lifelong project helped to document Paris during the nineteenth century, especially the city’s rapid changes from the 1850s to the 1870s, when Emperor Napoleon III and his prefect of the Seine, Baron Eugène Haussmann, transformed the city with new boulevards, green spaces, and public utilities, and fostered innovations in commercial and cultural practices. item.description: Stanford Events — IT Career Pathways highlights the diverse roles across our organization, connecting you with the people who do this work and the resources to help you follow in their footsteps. In this session, we’ll explore the dynamic, high-impact world of Data & Analytics. Have you ever wondered how to pivot from your current role into one where you work with data every day? Or are you looking to grow your career in Data & Analytics? Our panel of experienced data professionals from across Stanford will demystify their work through candid stories of challenges, breakthroughs, and discovery. You’ll gain insight into the mindset, skills, and wide-ranging opportunities within the field. Bring your curiosity and leave with ideas—and a blueprint—for your next steps in Data & Analytics. item.title: Public Lecture: Gravitational Wave Detection
item.description: Stanford Events — How do we detect tiny stretches of spacetime? Join us to learn how sensitive instruments are built to enable scientific discoveries! This lecture will be offered in a hybrid format, is open to all, and is recommended for adults and students in 9th grade and above. Title: Measuring the Impossible: How We Detected Gravitational Waves Speaker: Dr. Alexandra Mitchell (Stanford/KIPAC) Abstract: Two black holes collide over a billion light-years away, creating waves in the fabric of spacetime. But by the time those waves reach us, their effect is so small that they would change the light-years of distance by less than the width of a human hair. item.title: The Future of Decision-Making Conference
item.description: Stanford Events — About the event: AI-enabled decision systems are moving from labs to operations across military commands, intelligence analysis, crisis management, and clinical settings. The question is no longer if machines will inform high-stakes choices, but how to understand human judgment and accountability as they do, especially as many institutions fielding these systems lack empirical baselines and governance frameworks to manage them. The Future of Decision-Making Project (FODM), based at Stanford's Center for International Security and Cooperation, is a multi-year international research initiative examining the human dimension of decision-making in these high-stakes domains. FODM will host a public conference on October 28, 2026, bringing together scholars, practitioners, and operational experts to review the state of the field and future research directions. item.title: Planetary Science and Exploration Seminar, Martin Kihoulou - "Tectonic breathing of icy moon Europa: Could subduction- and rifting-like processes support habitability in the outer solar system?"
item.description: Stanford Events — Abstract: The geologically young surface of Jupiter’s icy moon Europa shows multiple lines of evidence for both divergent and convergent tectonic activity: dilation bands, where fresh ice has been emplaced, and regions interpreted as “subduction” zones, where ice appears to have descended under the surface. These motions are likely driven by cyclic global expansion and contraction of the ice shell resulting from long-term variations of Europa’s orbital eccentricity. We show that resulting vertical transport of chemical compounds across the ice shell possibly allows for transient habitable conditions within the subsurface ocean. The efficiency of this exchange depends on the amplitude and frequency of eccentricity variations, and we demonstrate that the present-day area of Europa’s dilation bands can only be explained by multiple episodes of ice shell thinning and thickening during Europa's surface age. item.title: Benjamin Yoel — International Pressure and Opposition to Democratic Backsliding
item.description: Stanford Events — Under what conditions do pro-democracy global actors support domestic opposition actors resisting democratic backsliding, and when does such support shape public opinion? This book project develops a theory of international rhetorical pressure that examines both the supply and demand of foreign engagement in backsliding contexts. On the supply side, it argues that international actors' public attention to democratic developments abroad is shaped by both domestic political developments and geopolitical ties. On the demand side, it suggests that foreign statements can shape public opinion toward pro-democracy movements. Drawing on an original dataset of US Secretary of State speeches, survey experiments, and elite interviews, the project shows that geopolitical interests often shape when international actors publicly address democracy abroad, but that when they do, foreign messages can meaningfully shape public opinion. item.description: Stanford Events — Join us for a film screening of Lithuania's submission for the Academy Awards with commentary from Maarja Merivoo-Parro, CEO of Vabamu Museum of Occupations and Freedom. How to Divorce During the War takes place in Vilnius, Lithuania in 2022. High-flying executive, Marija (Zygimante Elena Jakstaite), chooses the worst possible moment to inform her husband, Vytas (Marius Repsys), that she wants a divorce: just one day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Suddenly the couple must navigate the process of separation as it collides with a refugee and mid-life crisis. A struggling film director, Vytas is put into a tight spot by having to move in with his Russophile parents, while Marija struggles to find her footing as the war affects both her business and home life. As the reason for the divorce gradually becomes clear, the dissolution of Marija and Vytas’ marriage creates conflicts and opportunities for both of them, while also affecting their ever-observant young daughter, Dovile. item.title: Book Talk: Chrystia Freeland — Unreliable Boyfriend: An Insider's View of Dealing with a Chaotic Superpower, Plutocrats, and Other Complicated People
item.description: Stanford Events — How should allies deal with a superpower they can no longer rely on? Former Canadian Deputy Prime Minister Chrystia Freeland joins CDDRL to discuss her new book, "Unreliable Boyfriend: An Insider's View of Dealing with a Chaotic Superpower, Plutocrats, and Other Complicated People." Freeland has seen these questions from two sides. As a foreign correspondent, she covered the rise of Russia's oligarchs in the 1990s. As a senior Canadian official, she helped renegotiate the trade agreement between Canada, the U.S. and Mexico. The book draws on both careers to examine how power operates inside government, why trade, security and democracy can no longer be treated separately, and how democracies might build coalitions strong enough to resist authoritarian states and domestic oligarchs. item.title: Planetary Science and Exploration Seminar, Catherine Johnson - "Mercury’s Enigmatic Magnetic Field"
item.description: Stanford Events — Mercury’s interior structure and its magnetic field are unique among the terrestrial planets and moons of the Solar System. Its large metallic core (~83% of the planetary radius) formed under highly reducing conditions, requiring a core composition that includes substantial silicon and some, but more limited, sulfur and carbon. Mercury is also the only planet other than Earth to have both core and crustal magnetic fields. The core field constrains the present-day dynamo and crustal magnetization, if remanent, can constrain the dynamo history. The core field is dominantly dipolar, axisymmetric, asymmetric about the planetary equator, and ~100 times weaker than Earth’s field at the planetary surface. Structure beyond this simple picture is weak but exists, in particular a high-northern-latitude regional magnetic field anomaly spatially coincident with the topographic and gravity signature of Mercury’s Northern Rise.
